intro: A Babylonian healing ritual in Akkadian, copied at Ḫattuša, for removing the 'seizure' of li'bu-fever 'of the mountain'. A clay substitute of the patient, made with his urine, hair and nail-parings, is set riding on clay donkeys loaded with provisions, presented to the Sun-god Šamaš and sent out of the house to the open country, with incantations addressed to Šamaš, to the grain-goddess Nisaba (the flour) and to the ešegu-thornbush(?). The last paragraphs add shorter remedies against the same fever: a juniper-oil treatment with an incantation, amulets and a salve.

sections.title: Ritual with donkey figurines and a substitute figure against li'bu-fever

paras.en: To remove the seizure of li'[bu-fever] of the [moun]tain: you take the urine of a living donkey, (its) harness-strap(?) and the hair of its tail, and you mix the donkey's urine with clay from the tablet-house (the school). You knead(?) (it) and make two donkeys. You put the strap on (the figurine's) strap and the tail-hair on its tail. You make a saddle (lit. 'chair') for the DÚSU-donkey of … clay (ša IM i-ša-ri-im), and on the DÚSU-donkey you place a figure … of a substitute. The substitute figure: the urine of the man whom Namtar (the Fate-demon) has seized, the hair of his armpits, the hair of his chest and the parings of his nails you mix with that clay and make the figure. You clothe it in a garment and put a headdress on it; you set it riding on (the donkey). Two loaded(?) donkeys walk in front of the DÚSU-donkey: you fill one sack and place (it) on (the first); a sack that is full of flour you place on the second. You make (another figure) of clay, clothe it in a garment and put a wooden ŠU.KIN (a goad?) in its hand; you station it behind the donkeys and put a headdress on it. The substitute figure that rides the DÚSU-donkey you station with the donkeys, and you bring the figures of the donkeys up onto the roof before Šamaš. Flour, dates and mashatu-flour you [strew] as a strewn offering [before Šamaš; behind the strewn offering] [you station two donkeys before Šamaš]; [behind the donkeys you station a weapon]. [The exorcist speaks thus before Šamaš]:

'[Šamaš, lord of judgment and verdict are you]; above the counsel of kings, before [gre]at kings, you are great; you bring the case of those above to those below, [the ca]se of those below to those above. [Fo]r so-and-so, son of so-and-so, whose god is so-and-so, [whose goddess] is so-and-so, whom li'bu has seized — he does not know (it); [a living one(?)] has seized him — he does not know (it) …' [three lines lost] … [roam]ing … [one line lost] … not … has seiz[ed (him)] …

(For) as many days as … From the roof you [bring (it) down] and [take (it)], and bring the subst[itute] out to the open country. The patient (says) thus: 'Li'[bu], you were created(?) in my flesh …; to my substitute I (hereby) g[ive you]; [yo]u — be gone!' [You say to Šamaš: 'To the substitute of so-and-so, son of so-and-so, I am given, I am provisioned(?); be gone!' Over the patient you speak thus; with seven dried loaves you wipe him seven times.] Before Šamaš you place the figures of the donkeys in a basket; seven sila of flour, seven sila of mashatu-flour, seven sila of dates (and) seven sila of oil you pour out(?) on the ground; you have that man speak as follows:

'Nisaba, you are pure, who are set in the [lux]uriance(?) of the people! The god has fixed your destiny (as being) to release the curse. On this day — (you) who entered this house — I have laid (on you) the oath by the god: you are driven out, you have gone away! Do not linger! And behind those donkeys torch (and) SAG-vessel … have been made to pass(?); … you keep casting down(?) mankind.' You draw a design and speak thus: '[You are adj]ured: not […]! [By E]nl[il] you are [adj]ured: not […]! By Ninl[il], ditto, ditto! By Asalluḫi, ditto! By Baba, the bride, (and) Ningišzida, the throne-bearer: be led out! be ch[ased away]! be driven off! be [gone]! From this day, with his substitute and his likeness you are [provided(?)]. Your road is made straight — take (it)! […] … be far off(?), (go) empty-handed(?), g[o away]! By the oath of the great gods, be re[moved]! The design that is in your hand(?) — cross(?) (it), and do not come back, do not turn around; go away to where you have been driven!' You take (it) out of the house and bring (it) out to the open country; from the open country, going out to the ešegu-thornbush(?), you strew coarse flour, dates (and) mashatu-flour. Behind the (offering) arrangement you station two donkeys before Šamaš; behind the donkeys you station a weapon; behind the donkey on which the substitute figure rides you station a weapon. 'Šamaš, before you I am whole(?); behind you I am not whole(?). Šamaš, lord of judgment (and) verdict are you, above the counsel of kings, before great kings you are great; you bring the case of those above to those below, the case of those below to those above. So-and-so, son of so-and-so, whose god is so-and-so, whose goddess is so-and-so, whom li'bu has seized — he does not know (it); a dead one (or) a living one has seized him — he does not know (it); a ghost has seized him, a ghost of the family has seized him — he does not know (it); a roaming ghost has seized him — he does not know (it); a restless ghost has seized him — he does not know (it); namtaru, asakku, chills (šuruppû), ex[haustion] have seized him — he does not know (it); ardanānu(?), a dead one, an evil ghost have seized him — he does not know (it); Lamaštu, Labāṣu (and) Aḫḫāzu have seized him; ennungal(?), who strikes the forests, who loosens the skull, dries up the sinews (and) the palate(?), tears out(?) the heart, and makes his kidneys … (muštēmidu): trusting in Šamaš, I have put the oath of the great god(s) into his mouth.'

Before Šamaš the exorcist speaks thus: 'O ešegu, you are the offspring of Enlil! Because of so-and-so, son of so-and-so, whose god is so-and-so, whose goddess is so-and-so, whom namtaru, asakku, li'bu, a roaming ghost, a restless ghost (and) li'bu of the mountain have seized, I myself have seized you. Speak to Šamaš, plead(?) for him! Let the li'bu that has seized so-and-so, son of so-and-so, let (him) go, and I will let you go!' You pour oil on the ešegu; [that e]šegu you bind to a rush (Ú.AŠKI), you wrap its top all around and speak thus: 'The god has sprinkled(?) … upon you. Šamaš! Let l[i'bu] release the man, and I will release you!' In front of the rites of your release you place a dried (loaf) of one (sila), and you draw two (designs) of a cubit (each?), and you draw seven designs before the seven(?). Wherever there are designs you place a dried loaf of 〈one sila〉. You do not look behind you. You put the great oath of the gods into his mouth. As you enter the city gate, you throw flour on this side and that, and throw a strewn offering in the middle, and on the two doors of the gate you keep throwing (it) on this side and that, and (say): 'I have adjured you by the great gods who are in the ešegu: it shall not enter the open door! Go after her(?), to whom you are given(?) — be gone!' Into the flour that is poured out (as offering) you mix salt and cress.

(If) the 'seizure of the mountain' has seized him and seizes him (again) on the third day; (if) [it constantly brings(?)] on him a burning, [stro]ng fever and sweat [(and) he keeps having (it)?]; (if) it has become prolonged, and … has … him, (and) they seize him [(during?) his tr]eatment(?): you [ke]ep (ready?) one sila of juniper; you crush (it) (and) mix (it) with oil. They begin [his treatment]; they recite the incantation '[A]rābapura'(?). [When they are fini]shed, when his seizures [have left him(?)], you do not change the plant or the incantation; [you repeat (it) again and again], and [his treatm]ent will succeed.

… mūṣu-stone, isqūqu (coarse flour?), bronze dust from the face of a statue … [and MA.NU-wood: you wrap (them) in the wool of a lamb that has not known a male], [in an ulinnu-band from a she-kid that has not known a male], [white and black, you tie (it), put (it) on her(?) neck, and (the patient) will recover].

[If ditto: mūṣu-stone, the LIGIDBA-(stone?), 'sea-tooth' (ZÚ.A.AB.BA, coral?) (and) 'spittle of the River' (UŠ₁₂.dÍD) you crush together and mix with oil]; [you smear his temples repeatedly], [and anoint the soles of his feet, and he will recover].

[If ditto: you take the semen(?) (A.RI.A) of a creature (A.ZA.LU.LU)], [in … (ak ŠID) you wrap (it), (and) enclose(?) (it) in the skin of a fallen sheep], [put (it) on her(?) neck, and (the patient) will recover].
